story.headline: NVIDIA and Cisco Introduce USFP Optical Module Specification
story.summary: NVIDIA and Cisco have introduced the USFP optical module specification to cram 4x OSFP bandwidth density into a single OSFP-sized module. The hardware advance pushes AI networking fabrics to 12.8 Tb/s.

draft.body:
On October 12, 2026, NVIDIA and Cisco announced plans for a new optical module standard called the Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP) during the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit. The standard is engineered to support 400 gigabits per second (Gb/s) per lane electrical signaling across AI networking fabrics, as detailed in an announcement on the [NVIDIA Blog](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ocp-global-summit-vera-rubin-scale-ai-factories/). By fitting higher lane counts into an octal small form factor pluggable (OSFP) footprint, the architecture provides a roadmap to reach up to 12.8 terabits per second (Tb/s) of overall transceiver capacity.

As AI clusters grow in scale to train foundation models and serve multi-step agentic workflows, networking fabrics face severe density constraints. Expanding switches traditionally requires adding intermediate tiers of networking switches, optical links, and cabling, which drives up latency, complexity, and power consumption. The USFP initiative seeks to scale throughput per switch port rather than forcing data center operators to abandon the familiar pluggable transceiver deployment model.

[[FIG1]]

## Packing 400 Gb/s Per Lane into an OSFP Footprint

The USFP architecture introduces 400 Gb/s-per-lane electrical signaling while maintaining compatibility with systems operating at 200 Gb/s per lane, according to [NVIDIA Newsroom](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-and-cisco-introduce-new-pluggable-optics-form-factor-to-scale-ai-factories). The initial planned transceivers house 16 full-duplex lanes in an OSFP-sized module to deliver 6.4 Tb/s of aggregate capacity, doubling both the lane count and per-lane bandwidth compared to 200 Gb/s-per-lane optics.

Future revisions of the USFP specification are architected to support 32 full-duplex lanes, enabling a total module throughput of 12.8 Tb/s. According to NVIDIA and Cisco, USFP delivers four times the front-panel bandwidth density compared to traditional 200 Gb/s-per-lane pluggable optical modules. The design is intended for use in both network switches and SuperNIC network interface cards, enabling clusters to connect larger volumes of 1.6 Tb/s endpoints directly without introducing extra switching tiers.

In a post on [Cisco Blogs](https://blogs.cisco.com/news/cisco-and-nvidia-announce-usfp-expanding-the-path-to-ai-connectivity), Cisco highlighted that modern AI infrastructure demands continuous communication across accelerators, data stores, and execution environments. Bill Gartner, Cisco senior vice president and general manager of optical systems and optics, noted that scaling optics to 400 Gb/s per lane required moving beyond incremental tweaks to existing module designs while retaining the field serviceability and operational simplicity that operators depend on.

## Connector Mechanics and Thermal Design

To accommodate dense signal routing, USFP employs a new two-dimensional array connector designed with a two-step insertion mechanism, as reported by [Techzine](https://techzine.eu/news/infrastructure/144909/nvidia-and-cisco-develop-usfp-form-factor-up-to-12-8-tb-s-capacity/). The design delays electrical engagement until the module is seated inside the cage, which minimizes contact wear, maintains signal integrity, and provides consistent insertion force. While built for 400 Gb/s SerDes systems, the connector also improves signal performance for 200 Gb/s lanes.

[[FIG2]]

Thermal management is another key constraint in high-speed optics. The USFP standard supports power dissipation of up to 100 watts without requiring a dedicated embedded cooling circuit inside the module casing, according to [NVIDIA Newsroom](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-and-cisco-introduce-new-pluggable-optics-form-factor-to-scale-ai-factories).

Overall, the partners state that USFP achieves roughly 1.3 times the power efficiency of 200 Gb/s-per-lane optics. By streamlining signal processing architectures across optical configurations, the standard targets lower transmission latency alongside reduced energy consumption per gigabit.

## Multi-Source Ecosystem and Implementation Path

Rather than maintaining a proprietary interconnect format, NVIDIA and Cisco are collaborating with connector and cable specialists TE Connectivity and Amphenol, according to reporting by [Investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/company-news/nvidia-and-cisco-announce-new-optical-module-for-ai-data-centers-93CH-4944865). The companies are designing cages, connectors, and optical transceivers to build a multi-vendor supply chain, with plans to establish an open industry specification through an upcoming community-led multi-source project.

The USFP project also aligns with ongoing technical work between the two companies to guarantee interoperability between NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet systems and Cisco Silicon One architectures, as noted by [StreetInsider](https://streetinsider.com/Corporate+News/Nvidia+and+Cisco+unveil+new+USFP+optical+module+for+AI+data+centers/27174905.html). While Source 1 notes the OCP Summit took place at the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, third-party wire reports variously referenced San Francisco datelines; the official announcements originate from the OCP event floor in California.

Neither company has shared release dates, mass production schedules, or unit pricing for early USFP transceivers. However, by establishing connector and mechanical standards in open industry bodies, NVIDIA and Cisco are laying the structural baseline for 400 Gb/s-per-lane optical networks ahead of future accelerator generations.

faq.q: What is the USFP optical module specification?
faq.a: USFP stands for Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable. It is an optical module specification co-developed by NVIDIA and Cisco that supports 400 Gb/s per lane electrical signals, delivering four times the bandwidth density of standard 200 Gb/s-per-lane modules within an OSFP-sized footprint.

faq.q: How much bandwidth capacity does USFP deliver?
faq.a: Initial USFP modules feature 16 full-duplex lanes providing 6.4 Tb/s of capacity, with the architectural specification designed to scale up to 32 lanes for an aggregate throughput of 12.8 Tb/s.

faq.q: Who is manufacturing the hardware for USFP?
faq.a: NVIDIA and Cisco are collaborating with Amphenol and TE Connectivity to build module cages, connectors, and transceivers, with plans to formalize the standard through a multi-source agreement.

faq.q: When will USFP optical transceivers be available for purchase?
faq.a: NVIDIA and Cisco have announced the specification and architecture plans, but neither company has disclosed commercial availability dates or pricing.
